content_voiceover: This slide covers the genetics and classic presentation of Wilms tumor. On the genetic side, WT1 sits at chromosome eleven p one three and is associated with Denys-Drash syndrome and WAGR syndrome. WT2 sits at eleven p one five and is associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. TP53 mutations at seventeen p one three and FWT1 at seventeen q one two are also implicated in familial forms. On the clinical side, the classic presentation is a child brought in with a palpable abdominal mass, often found incidentally by a parent during bathing. Associated findings include hematuria, hypertension from renin secretion by the tumor, malaise, and fever. Fellows should recognize this constellation, a painless abdominal mass plus hypertension and hematuria in a toddler, as the textbook picture of Wilms tumor.
keypoints: WT1 at eleven p one three, linked to Denys-Drash and WAGR syndromes
WT2 at eleven p one five, linked to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Classic presentation, painless palpable abdominal mass in a toddler
Associated findings, hypertension, hematuria, malaise, fever
keypoint_voiceover: Two genes to anchor on, WT1 at eleven p thirteen tied to Denys-Drash and WAGR, and WT2 at eleven p fifteen tied to Beckwith-Wiedemann. Clinically, picture a toddler with an incidentally discovered abdominal mass, sometimes with hypertension from renin release and hematuria, that is your classic Wilms tumor vignette.
